## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This paper is best read as two papers sharing one dataset. The first is a large, precisely estimated, and robust descriptive null: across four graduating cohorts of roughly 200,000 New York City public high school graduates linked to National Student Clearinghouse records, the cumulative share of ethnoracially matched teachers over grades 9–12 shows no meaningful association with college enrollment, and that null holds with and without covariates, with and without the grades 9–11 GPA/attendance controls, in the single-school subsample, and for two-year and four-year enrollment separately. Paired with the paper's own sorting diagnostics (Tables 11–12), which show that student race and student need still predict matched-teacher share after school fixed effects, this is genuinely useful evidence about an unusual margin — a four-year cumulative dose in a large, choice-heavy urban district — and it is the part of the paper the field should absorb. The second paper is the subgroup story the abstract leads with, and it cannot currently be relied on: the abstract, results text, and two pages of discussion describe a negative relationship between same-race teacher share and GPA for Black students, but Table 6 as printed reports that coefficient as +5.13 (SE 0.86), the largest positive estimate in the table; the same paragraph calls the no-covariate GPA models null when every one is starred; the Black-student attendance result in Table 5 is described as negative when the table shows positive; and the introduction and discussion reverse the sign of the attendance-sorting result that the results section reports correctly. Add a sample size stated three incompatible ways (159,832 in the text, 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b, ~202,655 in every regression), cohort windows that disagree between table titles and table notes, a 'teachers of color' regressor that excludes Asian teachers despite the prose, coefficients interpreted at a 0-to-1 change in a share whose within-group standard deviation is 0.11–0.20, and college models that condition on mediators and on graduation, and the honest verdict is that the paper is useful with real caveats — sitting near the boundary with treat-with-caution. Cite it for the enrollment null and the sorting evidence, read every number off the tables rather than the prose, and do not cite the Black-student finding in either direction until an erratum resolves the sign.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

#### Key Strengths

- A well-powered, robust descriptive null on college enrollment: the all-student covariate-adjusted estimate is −0.007 (SE 0.007) and group-specific estimates are similarly indistinguishable from zero, stable across every specification, subsample, and enrollment margin the paper reports (Tables 8, A1–A5, Figure 1). Nulls at this precision on an outcome the field routinely invokes for teacher-diversity policy are worth having on the record.
- The sorting diagnostics (Tables 11a–d, 12a–d) are the most durable material in the paper: student race predicts matched-teacher share more strongly after adding school fixed effects, and within race, IEP status, ELL status, poverty, and prior GPA predict match. This is a quantified warning that within-school comparisons in high school matching studies compare systematically different students, and it should be cited by anyone designing such a study.
- The data asset and exposure construct are new and defensible: near-universe NYCPS student–course–teacher links across all four high school years (an average of 27 teachers per student), linked to postsecondary enrollment, with the same-race-match and teachers-of-color predictors run side by side on identical samples so readers can see they behave differently.
- The paper is candid about its causal status. It explains why the student fixed-effects strategy used in elementary settings breaks down in tracked, multi-section high schools, states plainly that the design does not support causal claims, and publishes sorting diagnostics that undercut its own interpretation.
- Specification transparency is good: every regression table names the estimator (reghdfe, mmqreg), the fixed effects, the clustering unit (12th-grade school, ~485 clusters), the full covariate list, N, adjusted R², and cluster counts. A replicator with data access could re-run the models.

#### Key Concerns

- The paper's signature subgroup finding is contradicted by its own table. Table 6 prints the Black-student GPA coefficient as +5.1294*** with covariates and +7.9322*** without, while the abstract, results, and discussion call it a 5.13-point decrease. Minus signs survive elsewhere in the same tables, so this is not an extraction artifact. Table 5's Black-student attendance result is likewise described as negative and significant but printed as +0.0108** / +0.0046 (ns). Until corrected, the paper's most quotable claim is unusable.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

- The prose is not a reliable guide to the exhibits. Beyond the sign conflicts: the no-covariate GPA models are called null when all five are significant; the Asian GPA magnitude (4.6) is quoted from the no-covariate column while the Latine one (3.64) is from the covariate column; the introduction and discussion say fewer days attended predicts more same-race teachers for Black and Latine students when Table 12 shows positive (Latine, significant) and null (Black), and the results section says so correctly; the Table 3a narration misstates the White, Latine, and poverty contrasts, with the Latine pair transposed; and coefficients on a 0–1 share are described as 'a change of 1 percent'.
- Sample and construct bookkeeping is inconsistent enough to block reuse of the paper's figures. The final sample is 159,832 in the text, 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b (whose subgroups sum to 157,601), and ~202,655 in Table 3a and every regression; cohort windows are 2017–2020 in the text and regression notes but 2016–2018 in the titles and notes of Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a; 'teachers of color' is defined as Asian/Black/Latine/Native, operationalized as Black/Latine/Native ('URM'), and described in Table 1b's note as Asian/Black/Latine; and the 184,287 reported college enrollees exceeds 83% of 202,655.
- The college-enrollment models condition on mediators and on graduation. Grades 9–11 GPA and attendance are outcomes of the same four-year exposure (Tables 4–7 treat them as such), and for Black students the enrollment coefficient is −0.090*** without those controls (Table A4) versus −0.020 (ns) with them (Table 8), so the subgroup result depends entirely on a modeling choice the paper mischaracterizes as merely 'understating' effects. The 'driven by mobile students' explanation compares Table A4 (no mediator controls) to Table A5 (with them), changing specification and sample at once. Requiring four years of NYCPS data and graduation also conditions on post-treatment outcomes that Gershenson et al. (2022) show matching affects.
- Reported magnitudes are extrapolations far outside the data. Every headline effect ('96% to 98% attendance', '4.6-point GPA increase') corresponds to moving a student from 0% to 100% matched teachers; the observed within-group SD of the share is 0.11 (Asian), 0.12 (Latine), and 0.20 (Black), so per-SD effects are roughly 0.2 percentage points of attendance and 0.3–0.4 GPA points on a 100-point scale (about 0.05 SD). The single significant college coefficient (Asian students, URM-teacher share, +0.060**) is one hit among roughly a hundred uncorrected tests, is null in its own no-covariate column, and is converted in the Policy section into a recommendation to recruit Asian American teachers even though the regressor excludes Asian teachers by construction.
- No data availability statement, no replication package, no documented access pathway to NYCPS or NSC data, no IRB statement, and one set of results reported only as 'available upon request'. The specification is transparent, but the analytic dataset is not reconstructible: numerator/denominator of the match share, treatment of co-taught sections and dropped multiracial teachers, the college-enrollment time window, NSC non-match coding, and the collapsing rule for time-varying poverty/ELL/IEP flags are all undocumented.

#### What to Rely On

- In NYC, cumulative four-year exposure to ethnoracially matched high school teachers is not associated with college enrollment conditional on graduation. This null is precisely estimated and survives every robustness check reported (Table 8; A1–A5; Figure 1). It is the paper's one load-bearing finding.
- Within-school sorting of students to same-race teachers is substantial in NYC high schools and runs on characteristics that predict outcomes: student race predicts matched share more strongly after school fixed effects (Tables 11a–d), and IEP status, ELL status, poverty, and prior GPA predict match within race (Tables 12a–d). Cite this as a methodological caution for any high-school matching study relying on within-school comparisons.
- Descriptive exposure facts for the nation's largest district: Black students average about 24% Black teachers and 35% Black/Latine/Native teachers; Latine students 14% Latine teachers; Asian students 13% Asian teachers; White students 75% White teachers despite being the smallest student group (Tables 1a/1b, text). Quote these from the tables, not the prose, and note the descriptive-table sample differs from the regression sample.
- Same-race match and exposure to Black/Latine/Native teachers behave differently as predictors and should not be treated as interchangeable constructs in this literature — for example, the URM-teacher share is negatively associated with GPA for every non-White group in Table 7 while same-race share is positive throughout Table 6.
- The design argument itself: the paper's explanation of why student fixed effects fail in tracked, multi-section high schools (Empirical Models section) is careful and can be cited as a statement of the identification problem.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'A negative relationship between same-race teachers and GPA (or attendance) for Black students.' Table 6 prints +5.13*** and Table 5 prints +0.011** / +0.005 (ns). Do not cite this in either direction until an erratum settles which of the text or the table is correct; the entire Discussion built on it is contingent on the same resolution.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

- 'Positive associations between same-race teacher share and GPA/attendance for Asian and Latine students.' As printed they are real but tiny once rescaled to one SD of exposure (≈0.2 pp attendance, ≈0.05 SD GPA), they appear on the same within-school variation the paper shows is sorted on ELL status, and GPA is a teacher-assigned outcome the paper never discusses as such — differential grading is as consistent with the pattern as any role-model mechanism.
- 'The null on college enrollment shows matching does not affect college-going.' It shows no association in a descriptive within-school comparison among students who persisted four years and graduated, with mediators controlled; it does not overturn Gershenson et al. (2022) or Delhommer (2022), which use stronger variation and include the persistence margin.
- 'Black students' results are driven by mobile students.' The comparison behind this (Table A4 vs. A5) changes both the covariate set and the sample; against the like-for-like Table 8 column 6 the Black coefficient was already null, so nothing is being explained.
- 'Teachers of color are positively associated with college enrollment for Asian students, supporting recruitment of Asian American teachers.' The regressor is the share of Black, Latine, and Native teachers, so the coefficient says nothing about Asian teachers; it is also the sole significant estimate among ~100 tests and is null in the adjacent no-covariate column.
- Any sample size, cohort window, or descriptive contrast quoted from the prose. The text's 159,832 students matches no table; table titles and notes disagree on 2016–2018 versus 2017–2020; the Table 3a narration is wrong for three of five contrasts. Use the regression tables' N (~201,000–202,655) and the 2017–2020 window from the regression notes.
- Any magnitude quoted as a per-unit coefficient (e.g., '96% to 98% attendance', '4.6-point GPA increase'). These are 0-to-100% extrapolations; rescale to one SD of the share before repeating, and note the 4.6 Asian figure is from the no-covariate column.
- The quantile-regression sensitivity result for college enrollment (Figure 1) and the selectivity results (Table 10). Quantile regression on a binary outcome adds nothing beyond the mean regression, and Table 10 pools enrollees at unranked institutions (about 36% of college-goers) with non-enrollees, reports no cluster counts, and prints its standard errors ambiguously.
- The novelty claim 'first study across all four years of high school'. Delhommer (2022) builds cumulative course-level match in Texas and Gottfried et al. (2022) examine course-level match across high school; the defensible novelty is the continuous four-year cumulative share estimated within schools in a single very large urban district.
- Several citations before repeating them: Blazar (2021) is given as 0.45 SD in the introduction and 0.25 SD later; Shirrell et al. is cited as 2023 but listed as 2024; Roksa & Velez (2012) is cited but absent from the reference list; the Gershenson et al. (2022) 'Black male teacher' framing and magnitudes should be checked at source.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Treat With Caution

This paper offers a useful descriptive extension of research on teacher ethnoracial matching by linking individual high-school teacher exposure to college enrollment among selected New York City public-school graduates. Its strongest surviving result is a small pooled conditional association between same-race exposure and enrollment in the reported adjusted models (p. 12, Table 8; p. 25, Table A3), not evidence that matching or teacher-diversity policies have no effect. My overall judgment is treat with caution: unresolved contradictions in the Black-student GPA finding, inconsistent sample documentation, and specification-dependent subgroup results undermine reliance on the central narrative as published. The literature and contribution reviews appropriately recognize the value of the question, data linkage, and urban setting; that value does not resolve the reliability problems identified by the methods, writing, and reproducibility reviews. Readers can cite narrowly specified results as reported associations, but should withhold the adverse Black-GPA conclusion and broad policy or mechanism interpretations pending clarification or replication.

#### Key Strengths

- Individual course-teacher records linked to National Student Clearinghouse enrollment records connect classroom exposure with postsecondary access, providing a useful NYC high-school extension with explicit attention to Asian, Black, and Latine students (pp. 2, 5-7).
- The descriptive framework is appropriate to the stated associational question: school and cohort fixed effects address stable school differences and common cohort shocks, school-clustered uncertainty is reported, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that the design cannot establish causation (pp. 6-7, 16-17).
- The exhibits disclose adjusted and unadjusted models, subgroup estimates, and bound sensitivity analyses; they permit meaningful checks that substantially qualify the headline account (pp. 10-12, Tables 4-9; pp. 24-26, Tables A1-A5).
- The conceptual discussion connects quantitative matching research with mentoring, institutional support, expectations, and qualitative accounts of teachers of color, while recognizing conflicting evidence and structural constraints (pp. 1-5). This is useful framing rather than evidence that a particular mechanism has been identified.

#### Key Concerns

- Central reporting conflicts are document-verifiable. The discussion describes a 'negative and significant relationship with GPA for Black students' (p. 19), but the adjusted Black same-race coefficient is printed as '5.1294***' with '(0.8581)' (p. 11, Table 6, column 6). Likewise, the attendance narrative says 'negative and significant' for Black students' exposure to teachers of color (p. 9), whereas the adjusted cell prints '0.0046' with '(0.0040)' and no significance marker (p. 10, Table 5, column 6). These disagreements establish unreliable reporting, not which version reflects the underlying analysis.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article does establish which version is right. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA on Black-teacher share as negative and significant in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26) plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting; the discussion's "negative and significant" GPA relationship (p. 19) is the correct reading. The attendance point stands: the adjusted Black-student cell, 0.0046 (0.0040), is not significant under either sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

- The analytic population and some estimands remain unresolved. The methods state 'Our final sample consisted of 159,832 students' (p. 6, exposure definition), whereas Table 8 prints '202,655' and '201,071' in its pooled N row (p. 12, columns 1-2). For college selectivity, the prose gives 'rankings for 118,289 students' but Table 10 prints 'N 201,370' (p. 13, selectivity discussion and table). The latter could reflect different outcome coding rather than an erroneous count, but nonenrollees and unranked institutions are not clearly accounted for; enrollment follow-up and exposure construction also lack sufficient detail (pp. 5-7, 13).
- The enrollment null is conditional and cannot bear the abstract's broad interpretation. For Black students, the reported same-race coefficient is -0.0903 (SE 0.0316) without academic controls versus -0.0195 (SE 0.0296) with them (p. 25, Table A4, column 3; p. 12, Table 8, column 6). The samples also differ. My methodological judgment is that conditioning on graduation and academic measures accumulated during exposure prevents interpreting these comparisons as total causal effects or a mediation test; school fixed effects do not remove within-school assignment confounding.
- The framing sometimes outruns both the measures and prior evidence. The regression exposure labeled teachers of color excludes Asian teachers (p. 5; p. 12, Table 9), and role modeling is hypothesized rather than observed (pp. 3-5, 17-19). The literature review's description of Gershenson et al. as exposure to a 'Black male teacher' (p. 1, introduction) also conflates teacher gender with the student subgroup emphasized in that study; its published abstract defines assignment to a Black teacher. Readers should consult that original source before repeating the comparison: [Gershenson et al., published abstract](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.20190573).
- The supplied article documents neither a replication package nor a followable restricted-data access procedure, and it leaves consequential coding choices unspecified (pp. 5-8, 13, 20). This limits independent resolution of the reporting conflicts; it is not criticism of keeping confidential student records private. Bound appendices were reviewed, but unbound online supplements and results available only upon request were unavailable and cannot be presumed to resolve these problems.

#### What to Rely On

- The published preferred model reports a small pooled adjusted same-race enrollment association: coefficient -0.0073, SE 0.0068 (p. 12, Table 8, column 2). The pooled academic-control variants are also small and unstarred (p. 25, Table A3). Cite this as a specification-specific reported association among the included graduates, with the unresolved sample documentation disclosed.
- The adjusted same-race attendance associations are positive for Asian and Latine students in the reported models (p. 10, Table 4, columns 4 and 8). These support a bounded descriptive pattern, not an established behavioral mechanism; the table notes include attendance controls overlapping the outcome period.
- The reported adjusted enrollment association for Asian students exposed to Black, Latine, and Native teachers is positive: coefficient 0.0604, SE 0.0241 (p. 12, Table 9, column 4). This qualifies the blanket enrollment-null account; it is neither an Asian-teacher matching result nor evidence of a causal benefit, and it warrants caution among the many subgroup comparisons.
- Student characteristics predict same-race exposure in the within-group assignment models: English-learner status is positively associated with exposure for Asian and Latine students, and IEP status is positively associated with exposure for Black students (pp. 16-18, Tables 12a-12c, column 3). These are documented conditional patterns, not proof of why assignments occurred or that sorting explains the outcome estimates.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Do not cite a negative Black-student GPA association as established: 'negative and significant' in the discussion (p. 19) conflicts with '5.1294***' in the adjusted table cell (p. 11, Table 6, column 6). Nor should the positive printed coefficient silently replace the narrative as the verified underlying result.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: the article's own appendix settles the sign.*

- Qualify any claim of no enrollment relationship or no policy effect. The abstract says enrollment 'was not related to the proportion of teachers of the same ethnoracial background nor the proportion of teachers of color' (p. 1), but the Asian broader-exposure cell is '0.0604**' (p. 12, Table 9, column 4), and the Black same-race result changes with academic adjustment (p. 25, Table A4; p. 12, Table 8). Nonsignificance in the preferred models is not evidence of causal ineffectiveness.
- Verify GPA effect-size translations before reuse. The Latine narrative associates '1 percent' with a '3.64-point increase' (p. 9), whereas Table 6 prints '3.6393***' per unit of a proportion (p. 11, column 8; exposure definition, p. 6). A one-percentage-point increase implies about 0.0364 GPA points, calculated as 3.6393 multiplied by 0.01, assuming the printed coefficient is correct.
- Treat role-model, sorting, mobility, and policy explanations as hypotheses. For example, 'the results for Black students are driven by mobile students' (p. 19) is not established by the already-unstarred main estimate '-0.0195' (p. 12, Table 8, column 6) versus '-0.0142' in the restricted sample (p. 26, Table A5, column 3). Neither a causal mediation claim nor effects of national teacher recruitment or college-faculty matching follow from these analyses.
- Do not lean on college-selectivity estimates or claims of robustness across exposure quartiles. The selectivity denominator is unexplained (p. 13, Table 10 and accompanying prose); the distributional analysis shifts from 'effects at specific places in the distribution' (p. 13) to 'any quartile of same-race teacher matching' (p. 14, discussion of Figure 1). My methodological judgment is that outcome quantiles do not identify exposure subgroups, and the reported binary-outcome implementation is insufficiently explained.

#### Verification notes

Checks used the full supplied paper and bound appendices, with visual inspection of the disputed outcome tables and relevant sensitivity exhibits. The checked sub-review claims below required no correction. Confirmation refers to the published record, not independent reproduction of the analysis.

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: the pooled adjusted enrollment coefficient and SE are -0.0073 and 0.0068 (p. 12, Table 8, column 2); pooled sensitivity estimates remain small and unstarred (p. 25, Table A3).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility: 'negative and significant relationship with GPA for Black students' (p. 19) conflicts with the positive printed '5.1294***' (p. 11, Table 6, column 6); the PDF confirms the sign, not the intended result.
- CONFIRMED — Writing/methods: 'negative and significant' Black attendance prose (p. 9) conflicts with '0.0046' and '(0.0040)' without a star (p. 10, Table 5, column 6); adjusted Asian and Latine same-race attendance entries are positive and starred (p. 10, Table 4, columns 4 and 8).
- CONFIRMED — Contribution/writing: the abstract's 'was not related' enrollment claim (p. 1) overlooks the Asian broader-exposure coefficient '0.0604**' with '(0.0241)' (p. 12, Table 9, column 4).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/reproducibility: 'final sample consisted of 159,832 students' (p. 6) is unreconciled with '202,655' and '201,071' (p. 12, Table 8, N row); 'rankings for 118,289 students' versus 'N 201,370' leaves the selectivity population unclear (p. 13, prose and Table 10).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: Black enrollment estimates depend on academic adjustment, -0.0903 (SE 0.0316) versus -0.0195 (SE 0.0296), with different samples (p. 25, Table A4, column 3; p. 12, Table 8, column 6); the nonmover estimate is -0.0142 (SE 0.0316), also unstarred (p. 26, Table A5, column 3).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: '1 percent' and '3.64-point increase' (p. 9) mis-scale the proportion coefficient '3.6393***' (p. 11, Table 6, column 8); the reviewer's one-percentage-point conversion is about 0.0364 GPA points.
- CONFIRMED — Literature: 'Black male teacher' (p. 1) misstates the predecessor's exposure; the [Gershenson et al. published abstract](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.20190573) specifies assignment to a Black teacher and separately identifies concentration of college results among disadvantaged male students.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility: the underlying computations and intended corrections cannot be recovered from the supplied article; no code or data package is documented there, and unbound supplements and upon-request results were unavailable.
